passages.title: The Last Public Living Room
passages.passage:
A. Twenty years ago it was fashionable to write the library's obituary. Once every text on earth could be summoned to a screen, the argument ran, a building full of paper would go the way of the telegraph office, and its staff would follow. The prediction was confident, widely repeated and wrong. In several large cities, visits to public libraries have actually risen over the very years in which book-borrowing fell. What the forecasters had failed to grasp was that a library had never chiefly been a warehouse for books. The books were the excuse; the building was the point.

B. Ask a librarian what the institution offers now and the first answer is rarely reading. It is room. A public library is almost the last indoor space in a modern city where a person may sit for six hours without being expected to buy anything, explain themselves or leave. Teenagers who cannot study in a crowded flat, freelancers who cannot afford an office, pensioners for whom the walk to the reading room is the day's only conversation: all of them are using the library for something other than its collection. One head of service calls her building, only half joking, the city's last public living room.

C. Around that core, the range of services has spread in directions that would have baffled an earlier generation. Branches now lend sewing machines, seeds, musical instruments and power tools. They house recording booths, language conversation circles and drop-in clinics where a bewildered resident is walked through an online tax form. Far from making the profession redundant, the flood of information has made it more demanding. Fetching a volume from a shelf was a modest skill; steering a nervous seventy-year-old past three fraudulent websites to the one genuine one is not. Scarcity, as one commentator put it, has simply changed sides: information is now abundant and judgement is what is rationed.

D. The real threat to the library, then, is not irrelevance but arithmetic. A council that took the obituaries at face value could see no reason to go on paying for a building whose supposed function had migrated online. One town in the north of England closed its branch and replaced it with a 'digital hub', a room of touch-screen kiosks staffed by nobody. Within eighteen months, and without any announcement, a desk with a person behind it had been reinstated. The kiosks had turned out to be used mainly to ask where the person was. The episode illustrates a wider difficulty: there is no line on a budget spreadsheet for 'somewhere warm to do your homework', and what cannot be counted is easily cut.

E. If the library survives, it will do so by looking less like a temple of books and more like a town square with a roof. That transformation carries its own risk. An institution that becomes a general-purpose welfare outpost, with a few shelves kept for decoration, may find it has lost the one thing nobody else was offering, which was the permission to sit quietly with a difficult book. Whether the future library is a workshop, a refuge or a reading room is not a question for technologists to settle. It belongs to the people who walk through the doors, and they have not stopped coming.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes a replacement for a library that was quietly undone?
questions.explanation: Section D: the branch became a 'digital hub' of kiosks, but 'within eighteen months, and without any announcement, a desk with a person behind it had been reinstated'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) argues that the librarian's job has become harder rather than unnecessary?
questions.explanation: Section C: 'Far from making the profession redundant, the flood of information has made it more demanding', contrasting fetching a book with steering someone past fraudulent websites.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains what the people who predicted the library's end had overlooked?
questions.explanation: Section A: 'What the forecasters had failed to grasp was that a library had never chiefly been a warehouse for books.'

questions.q: Which section (A–E) presents the library as a place where visitors are under no obligation to spend money?
questions.explanation: Section B describes 'the last indoor space in a modern city where a person may sit for six hours without being expected to buy anything'.

questions.q: Which statement best expresses the writer's overall argument?
options: Libraries should stop lending books and concentrate on providing social services.
Digital kiosks are a cheaper and more reliable alternative to trained librarians.
Public libraries are closing because fewer people want to read.
Libraries have outlived the prediction of their death because their real value was never the books alone.
questions.explanation: Every section returns to the same claim: the obituaries were wrong because the building, the space and the human help were the point, not the collection. Option B is a risk the writer warns against in section E, not a recommendation.

questions.q: What does the story of the touch-screen kiosks most strongly suggest?
options: Residents in the north of England are less confident with screens than elsewhere.
The council reopened the branch because of public protests.
What the town's residents had valued in the branch was a person, not access to technology.
The council had not installed enough kiosks to meet demand.
questions.explanation: The kiosks were 'used mainly to ask where the person was' and the desk came back without any campaign or announcement — the writer lets the reader conclude that human help was the service people had actually been using. Nothing is said about protests or the number of kiosks.

questions.q: In section D, the word "reinstated" is closest in meaning to:
options: redesigned
brought back
moved elsewhere
paid for
questions.explanation: To reinstate something is to restore it to its former position; the staffed desk that had been removed was put back.

questions.q: According to the passage, the digital hub cost the council less to run than the branch it replaced.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says the council 'could see no reason to go on paying' for the building, but it never states what the hub cost or compares the two. The reader may assume savings, but the text does not give the figure.

passages.title: Six Legs on the Menu
passages.passage:
In a warehouse on the edge of a mid-sized European city, several million crickets are being raised on vegetable trimmings that the supermarket next door would otherwise have thrown away. [1] Within six weeks the crickets will be roasted, ground and packed into a protein powder whose label makes no mention of legs.

The case for eating insects is, on paper, overwhelming. Crickets convert feed into body mass roughly twelve times more efficiently than cattle, need a fraction of the water and land, and produce almost none of the methane that makes beef so costly to the climate. [2] Around two billion people already eat insects as a matter of course, and in many of those cuisines a bowl of fried grasshoppers is a treat to be looked forward to rather than a hardship to be endured.

Why, then, has the industry grown so slowly in precisely the countries that could most easily afford to switch? The obstacle is not nutrition, nor safety, nor even price, which has fallen steadily as the farms have scaled up. It is disgust, and disgust, as psychologists have long observed, is not an argument that can be met with a better argument. [3] The reaction is learned early, reinforced by every cartoon in which a bug crawls out of a sandwich, and remarkably resistant to information.

The industry's response has been to make the insect disappear. Powders, protein bars, pasta with a discreet percentage of cricket flour: the strategy is to get the nutrition into the shopper without the shopper ever having to confront the animal. [4] A generation that grows up eating cricket crackers without a second thought may come to find the whole crawling question rather quaint. Critics, however, point out that concealment cedes the argument before it has begun. If the only way to sell a product is to hide it, its image has not improved; the problem has merely been outsourced to a label.

There is a further wrinkle on which enthusiasts prefer not to dwell. Most of the cricket powder now produced does not end up in human food at all, but in feed for pets and farmed fish, where nobody's stomach needs persuading. [5] Whether that counts as a success or a detour depends on what one thought the point was.

A. The arrangement suits both parties: the shop pays nothing to dispose of its waste, and the farm pays nothing for feed.
B. Nor is the practice anything like as exotic as diners in Europe tend to assume.
C. One cannot reason a person out of a feeling they were never reasoned into.
D. It is a patient strategy, and its real target is not today's consumer but tomorrow's.
E. The insect economy, in other words, is thriving, just not on the plates it was designed for.
F. Even so, the powder retains a faint nutty flavour that some tasters describe as pleasant.
G. This is why most of the farms remain small family businesses with a handful of staff.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: 'The arrangement' and 'both parties' refer back to the supermarket's trimmings feeding the farm; the sentence explains why each side benefits before the text moves on to what happens to the crickets.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: 'Nor is the practice ... exotic' adds a second point to the case for insects and is immediately supported by 'Around two billion people already eat insects as a matter of course'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: The sentence before says disgust 'is not an argument that can be met with a better argument'; C restates that idea as a maxim, and 'The reaction is learned early' then describes the feeling.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: 'A patient strategy' whose target is 'tomorrow's' consumer sets up the next sentence about 'a generation that grows up eating cricket crackers'.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: 'In other words' sums up the point that the powder goes into animal feed, and 'not on the plates it was designed for' leads straight into 'whether that counts as a success or a detour'.

questions.q: What does the writer imply with the final sentence, "Whether that counts as a success or a detour depends on what one thought the point was"?
options: Feeding insects to fish and pets was always the main aim of the cricket farmers.
The cricket farms are on the verge of going out of business.
Enthusiasts have deliberately misled the public about how much powder is produced.
The industry is making money without achieving the change in human diets it was originally meant to bring about.
questions.explanation: The powder is selling, so commercially it is a 'success'; but if the point was to get people eating insects, sales to pet and fish farms are a 'detour'. The writer leaves the reader to notice that the original purpose has been sidestepped. Nothing supports B, C or D.

questions.q: In the fourth paragraph, "concealment cedes the argument" means that hiding the insect:
options: gives up the argument without contesting it
wins the argument decisively
delays the argument until later
makes the argument more complicated
questions.explanation: To cede something is to surrender or give it up. The critics' point is that by hiding the insect, the industry admits defeat on the question of its image rather than fighting it.

questions.q: Most of the people who eat insects regularly do so because they cannot afford other food.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says that in many of those cuisines fried grasshoppers are 'a treat to be looked forward to rather than a hardship to be endured', which directly contradicts the idea that insects are eaten only out of poverty.

passages.title: A Ledger of Losses: What Translators Actually Do
passages.passage:
A. A literary translator I know is asked the same question at every dinner party: are the machines about to take her job? Her answer has been polished by repetition. They already do, she says, the part of it that was never the job. The guests usually laugh and move on; had they pressed her, they would have found that she meant it quite precisely, and that the remark contains most of what there is to say about translation.

B. The popular picture of the work is that of swapping words: a sentence goes in, its equivalent comes out, and the only skill involved is knowing enough vocabulary. But languages do not divide the world at the same joints. One has a single word for a colour that another splits into two; one obliges a speaker to say whether an event was witnessed or merely reported; one, like Vietnamese, folds the age and relationship of two people into the very pronoun by which they address each other, information that the English 'you' silently throws away. A translator therefore spends less time finding equivalents than deciding what to lose. Every translated page is a ledger of losses and compensations, and no two translators keep the same accounts.

C. Nor is there agreement about what the finished page should feel like. One school holds that a translation ought to read as though it had been written in the reader's own language, every seam invisible. The rival school insists that the reader should be kept aware of the text's foreignness, reminded on every page that it came from somewhere else and was made by someone unlike them. Neither camp has won, and in practice a translator's choice frequently owes less to principle than to the commission. A publisher wants a novel that will sell in airports; a university press wants one a scholar can cite with confidence; the same translator may serve both in a single year.

D. Wordplay is where these difficulties reach their limit. Take a joke that turns on two meanings of a single word. The translator has three options: explain it in a footnote, which is where jokes go to die; replace it with a different joke that does equivalent work, faithful to the spirit at the expense of the letter; or quietly drop it. A friend once translated a children's story in which a character's name was itself a pun. She invented a new name, with a new pun, in the target language. When the author was told, he replied that he wished he had thought of it first. That is a gracious response, but it leaves an awkward question hanging: whose page is it now?

E. Which brings us back to the machines. They perform impressively exactly where translation comes closest to substitution: manuals, weather forecasts, contracts, the great bulk of text that nobody reads for pleasure. They falter where translation comes closest to writing, because there the task is not to find the right word but to choose among several wrong ones. What remains for the human is the residue: the judgement about which loss is bearable, which betrayal is the lesser, which joke deserves to be rebuilt from scratch. My friend's dinner-party answer, in other words, was not a boast. It was a job description.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) suggests that a translator's approach may be shaped by who has commissioned the work?
questions.explanation: Section C: 'a translator's choice frequently owes less to principle than to the commission', followed by the contrast between a publisher and a university press.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) gives an example of an alteration that the original author welcomed?
questions.explanation: Section D: the translator invented a new punning name and the author 'replied that he wished he had thought of it first'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains how a single word in one language may carry information that another language leaves out?
questions.explanation: Section B describes the Vietnamese pronoun that encodes age and relationship, 'information that the English "you" silently throws away'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) identifies the kinds of text that computers translate well?
questions.explanation: Section E: machines 'perform impressively' on 'manuals, weather forecasts, contracts, the great bulk of text that nobody reads for pleasure'.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly concerned with?
options: Why jokes and puns should never be included in translated children's books.
Why the essence of translation lies in judgement about what to sacrifice, not in finding equivalent words.
How translators can protect their profession from being replaced by software.
The superiority of translations that keep the reader aware of the text's foreign origin.
questions.explanation: From the ledger of 'losses and compensations' to 'which betrayal is the lesser', every section argues that translating is deciding what to lose. The passage takes no side between the two schools in C and does not advise avoiding puns.

questions.q: When the translator says that machines already do "the part of it that was never the job", what does she mean?
options: Replacing words with their equivalents was never the real substance of translating.
Machines have taken over the badly paid work that translators used to refuse.
Translators have never been asked to translate manuals or contracts.
Her own job was abolished some years ago and she now works in another field.
questions.explanation: Section B dismisses 'swapping words' as the popular but false picture of the work, and section E says machines succeed only where translation is 'closest to substitution'. Put together, her remark means the mechanical part was never what translating really consisted of.

questions.q: In section E, "the residue" refers to:
options: the errors that machines leave in a text
the fee a translator receives
the original text before translation
what is left over after the mechanical part has been removed
questions.explanation: A residue is what remains after something has been taken away. Here it is the part of the job that survives once machines have done the substitution: the judgements.

questions.q: The writer believes the "invisible seams" approach produces better translations than the rival approach.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section C presents both schools and states that 'neither camp has won'; the writer describes the disagreement without saying which side he or she prefers.

passages.title: The Official and the Stubborn
passages.passage:
A visitor arriving in a city for the first time reads its streets before reading anything else, and the streets, whether or not anyone intended it, read back. [1] A grid of numbered avenues announces a place laid out in one go by people who prized efficiency over sentiment; a tangle of lanes named after long-vanished trades, Tanners' Row, Rope Walk, Candle Court, announces one that grew by accident and has chosen to remember it.

Who does the choosing varies more than one might expect. In some cities the power sits with a committee that meets four times a year and works through a list of the recently deceased; in others it belongs to the property developer, who names the roads of a new estate and shows a marked fondness for the trees that were felled to build it. [2] The results, however arrived at, are seldom neutral. A city that names a boulevard after a general has taken a position, and one that later renames it after a poet has taken another.

Renaming is where the politics show most clearly. After a revolution or a change of regime, one of the new authorities' first acts is commonly to overwrite the map, so that every journey across town becomes a small lesson in who now matters. [3] Older residents go on using the previous names for decades, taxi drivers keep both versions in their heads, and the city ends up with two layers of memory laid one over the other, the official and the stubborn.

There is also a quieter, more practical kind of naming, concerned less with honour than with being found. Ambulance crews dislike duplicate names, so a city with three Church Streets is under steady pressure to lose two. [4] The compromise reached in one European capital was to keep every name but let each district add its own number, producing addresses that are easy to deliver to and impossible to say aloud in a single breath.

Perhaps the most telling names, though, are the ones nobody chose at all. [5] A shortcut through a car park becomes 'the cut'; a corner where teenagers gather acquires a name that appears on no sign and on every phone; a bridge is known for a generation by the shop that once stood at its end. Officials may put up whatever plates they like. A street, in the end, is called what the people who walk along it call it.

A. Names are the most public form of memory a city possesses, and also the cheapest.
B. Elsewhere the choice was made centuries ago by nobody in particular and has simply stuck.
C. Yet the overwriting is rarely as complete as its authors hope.
D. The residents, who have written the old name on a thousand forms, dislike losing it even more.
E. These arise from use rather than from decision, and they are the hardest of all to remove.
F. The general, for his part, had never set foot in the city that honoured him.
G. Postcodes were introduced for much the same reason, though they honour nobody.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: 'Names are ... memory' explains how streets 'read back', and the following sentences give two examples of what a city's names reveal about its history.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: 'Elsewhere' adds a third answer to 'who does the choosing' after the committee and the developer; 'however arrived at' in the next sentence then covers all three.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: 'Yet the overwriting' picks up 'overwrite the map' and 'rarely as complete' is illustrated by the residents and taxi drivers who keep the old names alive.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: 'Dislike losing it even more' balances the ambulance crews' dislike of duplicates, and the two-sided objection is what makes 'the compromise' in the next sentence necessary.

questions.q: Which sentence (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: 'These' refers to 'the ones nobody chose at all', and 'arise from use' is shown by the shortcut, the corner and the bridge that follow.

questions.q: Which statement best captures the writer's central point?
options: Renaming streets after a revolution successfully erases the old regime from memory.
Street names are a record of who has held power in a city, but everyday use has the final say.
Cities should adopt numbered grids because they cause the fewest arguments.
Most street names are chosen by property developers with little regard for history.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from official naming and political renaming to the 'stubborn' layer of memory and the unofficial names that 'are the hardest of all to remove', ending with the claim that a street is called what its walkers call it. D is contradicted by the third paragraph.

questions.q: What does the writer imply by saying that a city which renames a boulevard after a poet "has taken another" position?
options: Cities should avoid naming streets after any real person.
Streets named after generals are usually renamed within a generation.
Choosing a poet over a general is itself a political statement, not a retreat from politics.
Poets are generally more popular with naming committees than generals.
questions.explanation: The sentence pairs the two acts as parallel: if honouring a general 'has taken a position', replacing him with a poet is not neutral either but a second position. The passage says nothing about popularity, timing or a ban on real names.

questions.q: In the final paragraph, "the most telling names" means the names that are most:
options: widely used
recently invented
difficult to pronounce
revealing
questions.explanation: 'Telling' as an adjective means significant or revealing; these unofficial names show most clearly how a city really thinks of itself.
